# Design Levers {#sec-levers-ch}

A solar project is a long list of decisions, and almost all of them fall into six groups. How much ground to take. Which ground. What to build on it. What grows there and how the place is run. Who owns it. What everyone signs. These are the **[design levers](terminology.qmd#term-design-levers)**, and they are the only things anyone can actually change.

Everything else in this lexicon follows from these six. The [design pressures](design-pressures.qmd) are the forces arguing over how each lever gets set, and the [restorative functions](restorative-functions.qmd) are what the settings produce.

Two of the chapters after this one need a word of explanation, because they are different kinds of thing. [Scale](scale-transect.qmd) gets a chapter because that one lever shapes so much else, and it is laid out as five reference points along the range of project sizes, from a farmstead array to a regional complex. The [farming axis](farming-axis.qmd) gets a chapter because it is not a lever at all. It is what siting, structure, and management produce together, recorded as six positions that describe what happened to the farming on the ground the array took. Most public argument about solar on farmland is really an argument about the farming axis. The other five levers are worked through here.

![**The six design levers.** Six sliders on a rail, each with what it decides and what it can deliver underneath: scale on its own behind a rule, then siting, structure, and management, then ownership and contracts. The handles sit at different heights because a lever is something that gets set. Where each one sits here is arbitrary and describes no particular project.](../figures/fig_design_levers.svg){#fig-design-levers}

## The levers {#sec-levers}

::: {.lever-table}
| Lever | What it decides | What it can deliver |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Scale** | how much ground the project takes · the capacity it is filed at, and the [zone](scale-transect.qmd#sec-zones) that follows · [interconnection](terminology.qmd#term-interconnection) posture, from [behind-the-meter](terminology.qmd#term-behind-the-meter) to transmission · whether to build once or phase several arrays | the transect position, and how much of every other lever is left |
| **Siting** | which ground the array takes, and where on the parcel · whether it stands upslope or downslope of the problem it might fix · how near it is to the fields it might serve · whether a landscape carries a few large arrays or many small ones | water quality, habitat context, service to nearby fields |
| **Structure** | mounting type and [clearance](terminology.qmd#term-clearance) · [row spacing](terminology.qmd#term-row-spacing) and [ground coverage](terminology.qmd#term-gcr) · [pore space](terminology.qmd#term-pore-space) · [module technology](terminology.qmd#term-module-technology) · grading and site works · the built half of the edge: setback, berm, wall, fence line | microclimate, room to farm, light to the ground layer |
| **Management** | the [ground layer](terminology.qmd#term-ground-layer) and how it is established · the mowing and grazing calendar · [stocking density](terminology.qmd#term-stocking-density) · [tracking and curtailment](terminology.qmd#term-tracking-curtailment) · construction sequencing and traffic lanes · the planted half of the edge: hedgerow, buffer, [screening](terminology.qmd#term-screening) | soil and carbon, habitat, most of the water balance |
| **Ownership** | who holds the asset: owner-operator, landowner, developer, utility, cooperative, or shared · co-ownership or an equity stake in place of a rent | a share of generation revenue for the people on the ground |
| **Contracts** | lease terms and duration · [offtake](terminology.qmd#term-offtake) structure · interconnection posture · the [community-benefit](terminology.qmd#term-community-benefit) instruments · easements · the [decommissioning](terminology.qmd#term-decommissioning) bond | the community function, and durability for everything above |
: The six design levers and the decisions inside each. Scale sets the frame. The three below it are physical and limited by how much ground there is. The two institutional levers are not. {#tbl-levers}

:::
Two things look like levers and are not. What a project is *aiming at* is a goal, not a decision about the project itself, so it counts as a pressure: [restorative goals](terminology.qmd#term-restorative-goals). What the ordinance requires is not chosen by anyone building the project, so it is a pressure too: [policy and permission](terminology.qmd#term-policy-permission). Both are covered in §-@sec-pressures-ch. Mixing goals and rules into a list of actual choices puts three different kinds of thing under one heading.

::: {.callout-note}
## Scale limits every other lever

Scale comes first because it limits every other lever, and it gets a chapter of its own (§-@sec-transect). It does no restorative work by itself. No field gets repaired and no flock gets fed because a project is 40 acres instead of 400. For some people scale is a choice, and for others it is a given. A farmer with one parcel and a distribution line at the road has very little say over it, while a developer assembling acreage near a [substation](terminology.qmd#term-substation) has a great deal. Both are choosing, and only one of them knows it.

How much each of the other five levers can still deliver once the size is settled is the subject of §-@sec-modes.
:::

## The physical levers: siting, structure, and management {#sec-lv-physical}

**Siting** is the choice of ground. Where a designer still has that choice, it is the most powerful of the six levers, though it decides a project's place on the [farming axis](farming-axis.qmd) only together with structure and management (§-@sec-farming-axis). It is also the first lever to disappear as projects get bigger. Where an array goes decides whether it can help water quality at all, because the two ways of doing that need opposite ground. [Avoided loading](terminology.qmd#term-fn-hydrologic) needs the field that is leaking the nutrients, while interception needs the ground between that field and the water [@schulte2017]. Placement also decides whether a pollinator planting helps anyone. A pollinator forages within roughly 1.5 km, and about 3,500 km² of US farmland lies within that distance of existing and planned solar [@walston2018]. And good siting costs less than people tend to assume: planning all of New York's 2050 solar build around biodiversity came to just 0.17% more than the least-cost plan [@gallaher2026].

**Structure** is the hardware and how it is laid out. It controls the [microclimate](terminology.qmd#term-microclimate) under the panels entirely. The shade, the lower vapor-pressure deficit (less drying stress on plants), and the warmer nights all come from the geometry, not from anything growing. Those effects show up in the water, ecology, and agriculture functions rather than as a function of their own (§-@sec-functions). Row spacing is not purely a structural decision, because crops differ in how much shade they will accept in exchange for relief from heat. The spacing and the ground layer are really one decision made by two parties [@weselek2019]. Structure also decides how much earth gets moved. That is the least visible choice of all and one of the most important, because a [racking](terminology.qmd#term-racking) system chosen on cost can set a site's soil carbon for thirty years before anyone picks a seed mix (§-@sec-fn-agricultural).

**Management** is what grows underneath and how the place is run, from the first day of construction to the last year of the lease. It carries the soil and its carbon, most of the habitat, and most of the water balance. It also starts earlier than people expect. The order of construction, and whether crews keep to set traffic lanes, decide how much of the original soil survives to be managed at all. Management is the only lever that can still be changed after the array is built, and that cuts both ways. A planting that was right in year one can be wiped out in year four by a contractor doing exactly what the maintenance schedule says [@blaydes2022].

The edge of a site is split between structure and management on purpose. A berm, a wall, or a fence is built. A hedgerow is planted, and has to be kept. The two fail differently: the berm will still be standing in year twenty whether or not anyone looked after it, and the hedgerow will not. A project that promises to screen the view with plantings alone has promised something that comes with a maintenance bill.

Scale does not limit these three equally. As a project grows, siting narrows and management widens, and the two trade places at A3 (§-@sec-siting-latitude).

## The institutional levers: ownership and contracts {#sec-lv-institutional}

**Ownership** is who holds the asset. It settles who gets to make the other decisions and who keeps what the array earns. An owner-operator, a cooperative, and a utility want different things, and the difference shows up on the [ground layer](terminology.qmd#term-ground-layer), not only in the books. [Barnyard shelter solar](archetypal-forms.qmd#arch-barnyard) is the clearest small-scale example. It is [restorative](terminology.qmd#term-restorative) because the person who owns the array also owns the animals under it, so no agreement was needed to line their interests up.

Ownership also changes more than any other lever as projects get bigger, and it changes in only one direction. At the [farmstead](terminology.qmd#term-a1), the array belongs to the farmer. At the [commercial](terminology.qmd#term-a2) and [community](terminology.qmd#term-a3) sizes, it belongs to the landowner, or to a community-solar arrangement with many small owners. At A4 and A5, it belongs to developer capital and then to a utility or an independent power producer, and the person on the ground holds only a lease.

The money from selling the power moves with ownership, and that money is the largest thing an [agrisolar](terminology.qmd#term-agrisolar) project creates. A lease pays for the use of the ground. It is not a share of what the array sells. So a landowner earning three to four times what the crop used to return per acre [@sturchio2025croplands] is still being paid for land, not for electricity. **Whether a project is restorative depends partly on who owns it, and a generous lease does not settle that question.**

That is why co-ownership, a community-solar subscription, or an equity stake in place of rent count as restorative tools and not just goodwill. Each one keeps part of the power revenue with the people hosting the array. Ownership produces no [restorative function](terminology.qmd#term-restorative-function) of its own. What it decides is who benefits from the functions the other levers produce, which is why the [community and economic function](terminology.qmd#term-fn-community) is most at risk when the owners live far away and strongest when ownership is local or shared.

**Contracts** are what the parties actually signed. This lever carries the [community and economic function](restorative-functions.qmd#sec-fn-community) almost single-handedly, and it is also what makes the other five last. The clearest published example works through contracts alone: solar lease income can pay for a conservation practice that federal biofuel policy had made too expensive to keep [@sturchio2025croplands]. No ground was chosen and no hardware was changed. The restoration happened in a contract, and contracts are the lever most often left on the table.

Contracts matter this much because the levers are fixed at very different times. Scale and siting are settled once. Structure is fixed on the day the array is built. Ownership changes hands over decades and contracts over years, while management can change next season. Stewart @brand1994, following Frank Duffy, describes a building as a set of layers that last different lengths of time, and argues that a design works when the fast layers can move without tearing the slow ones. @habraken2002 adds that each layer has its own decision-maker. Here management is the fast layer, and so the fragile one. It lasts only as long as somebody is paying for it and somebody else is checking on it, and both of those are contract questions. Choosing a seed mix is a management decision. Whether that planting survives to year twenty is a lease question.

Designed landscapes fail this way all the time. The Landscape Architecture Foundation reports that parts of many projects fail within a year or two, because the maintenance crew had no say during design and the designer's job ended at the final walkthrough [@douglas2015]. A solar project can be sited perfectly, built correctly, and planted well, and still be gravel in fifteen years, because the levers that would have kept it planted were treated as paperwork instead of design.

Which of the six levers a project relies on to do its restorative work is called its [restoration mode](terminology.qmd#term-restoration-mode). That choice matters enough to get a chapter of its own (§-@sec-modes).
